micro-epidemiology: What do the Greek roots of epidemiology mean?
The science of what falls upon people
In the five W's, what does Why cover?
Causes, risk factors and modes of transmission
Which use of training ranks diseases by who gets them and who dies?
Disease prioritization
Who first explained disease rationally, by environment and host?
Hippocrates
Who pioneered tabulating mortality as rates, ratios and proportions?
John Graunt
Who is the father of modern vital statistics?
William Farr
Who is the father of field epidemiology?
John Snow
What did Doll and Hill link in 1950?
Smoking and lung cancer
What did epidemiology help eradicate in the 1960s and 1970s?
Smallpox
What does genomic epidemiology monitor?
The genetic makeup of pathogens
Which branch describes disease by person, place and time?
Descriptive epidemiology
Which branch tests a hypothesis linking exposure and outcome?
Analytic epidemiology
What is the typical descriptive study design?
Community health survey (cross-sectional)
Name the typical analytic study designs.
Cohort, case-control and experimental
What is the triad of descriptive epidemiology?
Person, place and time
What is the triad of analytic epidemiology?
Host, agent and environment
What is a secular trend?
Disease occurrence over a prolonged period, usually years
Which kind of agent is tobacco?
Chemical
Where do vectors, vehicles and reservoirs belong in the triad?
Environment
What is a map of where cases lived and worked called?
A spot map
A questionnaire in a foodborne outbreak draws on which data source?
Individual persons
Stream samples and air-quality sensors are which data source?
The environment
Cigarette sales and intoxicated-driver arrests are which data source?
Nonhealth-related (financial, legal) records
What is surveillance for?
Facilitating prevention and control of disease
Which surveillance characteristic finds individual persons with disease?
Sensitivity
Which surveillance characteristic excludes persons without disease?
Specificity
Which surveillance characteristic pictures the temporal trend accurately?
Representation
Which surveillance uses staff to contact providers regularly?
Active surveillance
Which surveillance is most common but may under-report?
Passive surveillance
Which surveillance uses a prearranged representative group of reporters?
Sentinel surveillance
Which surveillance defines cases by clinical features alone?
Syndromic surveillance
What is a surveillance indicator?
A measurable factor estimating a health problem's size
What makes a disease reportable?
A law requires reporting it to authorities
Why are diseases made notifiable?
Contagiousness, severity or frequency
Which United States system collects notifiable disease data?
National Notifiable Diseases Surveillance System
Which diseases are reported by telephone?
Rubeola and pertussis
Which diseases are reported as total numbers of cases?
Chickenpox and influenza
Where is cancer reported?
State cancer registries
What does morbidity refer to?
Having a disease or a symptom of disease
Which two measures quantify morbidity?
Incidence and prevalence
What is the numerator of incidence?
New cases during the time period
Which measure is the odometer?
Prevalence
Prevalence depends on incidence and what else?
Duration of illness
Which mortality rate compares health status between countries?
Infant mortality rate
How is the case fatality rate calculated?
Deaths divided by total cases
What are exposures linked to a difference in risk called?
Risk factors
What does causation imply beyond association?
A true mechanism from exposure to disease
What sits at the base of the pyramid of associations?
Chance
Which Hill criterion requires exposure before disease?
Temporal sequence
Which Hill criterion is a dose-response relationship?
Biological gradient
Which Hill criterion is the same finding across studies and populations?
Consistency
Which Hill criterion is a very high or very low relative risk?
Strength of association
What is an endemic disease?
One found at chronically low levels in a population
What is a sporadic disease?
One occurring at irregular intervals or as isolated incidents
What is a pandemic?
A worldwide epidemic
What is herd immunity?
The number or percentage of immune persons in a population
What is the basic reproduction number?
Cases one case generates in a susceptible population, no interventions
Which epidemic type has exposure within one incubation period?
Point (common source)
Which epidemic type spreads person to person?
Propagated
Which epidemic type starts as common source and then propagates?
Mixed
What is the first step of an outbreak investigation?
Establish the existence of an outbreak
What is the last step of an outbreak investigation?
Communicate findings
Which design found Hotel A's lobby a Legionnaires' risk factor?
Case-control study
Which public health approach step asks what the cause is?
Risk factor identification
What is epidemiology's main contribution to policy?
Evidence
What is the first step of the policy cycle?
Assessment of population health
How did the 1994 report reframe youth smoking?
As a community and population issue
Which application studies hazardous waste sites and pollution?
Environmental epidemiology
